d: Operating income (operating revenue minus operating expenses) as a share of operating revenue. It leaves out income from investments, donations and other nonoperating sources.
Net income, including investment income, donations and other nonoperating revenue, as a share of total revenue.
A hospital's list prices for everything it provided, before any discount. Few payers pay them; they are the starting point for negotiated and government rates.
What a hospital expects to collect for patient care after discounts to insurers and government programs, charity care and bad debt are taken off its gross charges.

t: Charges per dollar of net revenue
d: Gross charges divided by net patient revenue. A value of 4.0 means the hospital listed $4 in charges for every $1 it expects to collect.
p: Charges per dollar of net revenue

d: The share of a hospital's gross charges billed to each payer: Medicare, Medi-Cal, private insurance, county programs and others. It is based on charges, not on what each payer actually pays.
Care a hospital provided free or at a discount under its financial assistance policy, to patients it judged unable to pay.
On this site, bad debt plus charity care, as a share of gross charges.
The share of a hospital's gross patient revenue that comes from outpatient care (visits, procedures and tests without an overnight admission).
A hospital that provides round-the-clock inpatient medical and surgical care. The comparisons on this site leave out psychiatric, rehabilitation and long-term acute care hospitals.
On this site, a hospital that qualifies for Medicare disproportionate share hospital (DSH) payments, which go to hospitals treating a large share of low-income patients.
A small rural hospital with no more than 25 inpatient beds, usually far from another hospital, that Medicare pays based on its costs.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services' Overall Hospital Quality Star Rating: one to five stars summarizing measures of mortality, safety, readmissions, patient experience and timely care. Hospitals that report too few measures get no rating.
An inpatient stay weighted by how resource-intensive the patient's condition is, so a hospital treating sicker patients can be compared with one treating healthier ones.
What commercial insurers paid divided by what Medicare paid for comparable care at the same hospital. 2.0 means commercial insurers paid twice Medicare's rate.
California's Medicaid program, which covers people with low incomes. Most members are enrolled in managed care plans.
The part of an employer plan's premium that the employee pays, usually through payroll deduction.
What a person pays for covered care each year before the plan starts paying, apart from services the plan covers in full.
A plan whose deductible is at least the minimum the IRS sets for pairing it with a health savings account.
California's health insurance marketplace under the Affordable Care Act, where people without job-based coverage buy plans, often with federal and state help.
The second-lowest-cost Silver plan available in an area. Federal premium tax credits are calculated from its price.
A federal subsidy that lowers Marketplace premiums for eligible people based on income. California adds its own help for some enrollees.
An office within HCAI, created by state law in 2022, that measures health spending in California and sets and enforces limits on how fast it may grow.
OHCA's limit on yearly growth in health spending per person, starting at 3.5% for 2025 and stepping down to 3.0% by 2029.
Spending divided by the number of people covered, for a year, so markets and regions of different sizes can be compared.
One of the 19 geographic areas Covered California uses to set premiums. OHCA reports spending using the same regions.
The Urban Institute's measure of what a family needs to cover essentials without hardship and to save for emergencies and the future. It is set higher than the federal poverty line.
The California Department of Health Care Access and Information, which collects hospitals' annual financial disclosures and publishes the Hospital Measurement dataset used for prices on this site.
The Insurance Component of the federal Medical Expenditure Panel Survey: a yearly survey of private employers on premiums, contributions and deductibles, with estimates for every state.
